rashi:a1.1: But with regard to the offspring of a guilt offering’s substitute, there is no burnt offering status for its mother: the first consecration, by whose force they all came, was designated as a guilt offering and was sacrificed as a guilt offering; it was not a burnt offering, neither it nor its value. In the Jerusalem version, the beginning of our passage [on 18b] goes back and asks, “And it is wholly burnt on the fires: is that the statement of all?” as a question, that is: why do the Rabbis not disagree about the offspring of substitutes as they do about the offspring of a burnt offering?
rashi:a1.2: And it is Rabbi Elazar [Rashi: “R. A.”; on Rabba bar bar Ḥana’s answer, 18b]: but according to the Rabbis it is sold; and the same applies to the offspring of a burnt offering’s substitute, and the first clause is Rabbi Elazar’s.
rashi:a1.3: The substitute of a burnt offering [on Rava’s answer, 18b]: it is second to that first animal that he designated, and the first one he designated was a male and was sacrificed. Therefore the offspring of its substitute is sacrificed too, etc.
rashi:a1.4: There is burnt offering status for its mother: in the bird burnt offering; moreover, its value stands to be a burnt offering. Therefore sanctity descends on its body, since we find its counterpart in a bird, which is sacrificed, and that is why the offspring is sacrificed. But with the offspring of a guilt offering’s substitute, there is no burnt offering status on the first animal, the mother of them all, by whose force it comes, and it was sacrificed as a guilt offering; and we do not find a guilt offering’s substitute sacrificed as a burnt offering. Therefore sanctity descends on the substitute only for its value, and that is why the offspring is not sacrificed.
rashi:a3.1: If it remained after Passover, etc.: for a Paschal offering during the rest of the year is a peace offering, as we say in Menaḥot at the end of chapter HaToda (Menaḥot 83b). But it itself is not sacrificed as a peace offering. Although peace offerings come from females, these, since they became disqualified because of their sanctity and are not fit for a Paschal offering, are pushed away from being peace offerings too.
rashi:a3.3: It itself is sacrificed as a peace offering: even though there is no peace offering status for its mother, since it was consecrated as a Paschal offering.
rashi:a4.1: After Passover is different, as a leftover Paschal offering: for example, if he designated a Paschal offering and achieved atonement with another, and this one was left over, it is sacrificed as a peace offering. Therefore this one, left over after Passover, has peace offering status on it: the name of Paschal offering departs from it and the name of peace offering takes effect on it, except that it cannot be sacrificed as a female, since it came by the force of a Paschal offering.
rashi:a5.1: If so: if Rabbi Elazar’s [Rashi: “Rabbi Eliezer”] reason is that there is peace offering status for its mother, let him also disagree in the first clause, where it gave birth before Passover, and let Rabbi Elazar say that the offspring itself is sacrificed as a peace offering. For before Passover too, if one slaughtered the Paschal offering for the sake of a peace offering it is valid, since a Paschal offering during the rest of the year, not on the fourteenth of Nisan, is a peace offering. Hence there is peace offering status for its mother.
rashi:a6.1: Abaye said: nobody disagrees at all: Rabbi Elazar’s reason is not that there is peace offering status for its mother. Rather, his reason in all these cases is that it is learned as a tradition: to the place that the leftover goes [the offspring goes]. If he designated two animals as a guarantee, or if one was lost and he designated another and achieved atonement with the other, and then the first was found, then the offspring goes to the place that this leftover goes. Therefore, with one who designates a female for a burnt offering: just as, if he designated a burnt offering and achieved atonement with another, the second is sacrificed as a burnt offering, since they are gift offerings and both are fit, so the offspring of the burnt offering, where he designated a female for a burnt offering, is sacrificed too, like the leftover. With a guilt offering too: since a leftover guilt offering grazes, the offspring of a guilt offering’s substitute grazes as well. And with a Paschal offering, after Passover: since the law of a leftover Paschal offering is to be sacrificed as a peace offering from the outset if he achieved atonement with another, the offspring too is sacrificed as a peace offering. Before Passover, the leftover is fit for nothing: for example, if he designated two Paschal offerings as a guarantee, they are not fit as peace offerings from the outset, since unspecified they stand for the Paschal offering, and the one of them that is left over is not fit for a Paschal offering, as he may not sacrifice two Paschal offerings. Therefore the offspring of the Paschal offering too is fit for nothing; rather it follows its mother, which is consecrated for the value of a Paschal offering, and this one too is consecrated for the value of a Paschal offering.
rashi:a10.1: If he left it out, it is left out: one who consecrates a pregnant animal and leaves its fetus out for a different sanctity, it is left out. Evidently they are two bodies. Therefore, even when he did not leave it out, it is not the mother’s body and does not come by the mother’s force, and the sanctity of a Paschal offering takes effect on it in its own right.
rashi:a11.1: It and its offspring: implies that both existed at the time of the consecration, since it does not teach, “One who designates a female for his Paschal offering, it grazes; if it gave birth to a male, it grazes,” as it taught above.
tosafot:a4.1: But here, where there is no peace offering status for its mother: here we can properly sustain both versions [of Rashi’s explanation of “burnt offering status for its mother,” on 18b], since there are no peace offerings from birds, and at the start of the consecration it was not designated for a peace offering.
tosafot:a5.1: If so, let him also disagree in the first clause: Rashi explained (first version): if it gave birth before Passover, let Rabbi Elazar [Tosafot: “Rabbi Eliezer”] say that the offspring itself is sacrificed as a Paschal offering, since there is Paschal status for its mother, except that it cannot be sacrificed. Here we cannot sustain Rashi’s first version above, that bird burnt offering status for its mother [counts], since here no Paschal offering comes from a female, as there is no Paschal offering from birds. But the second version works well, since at the start of the consecration it was designated for a Paschal offering, and he should have said that the offspring is sacrificed as a Paschal offering. And if you will say: let him answer that we need Paschal status for its mother somewhere, and we do not find it here, since there is no Paschal status by which a female itself is sacrificed, and that is why the offspring itself is not sacrificed as a Paschal offering — from here the RaMaR says that we never say that bird burnt offering status for its mother helps to make the offspring itself fit, and wherever we find this expression we will explain it, with God’s help. And in the first clause he explained well.
tosafot:a5.2: If so: And if you will say: what is the “if so” here? He could just as well have challenged directly from the mishna: why is it that with one who designates a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth, Rabbi Elazar said its offspring itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering, while here, with a Paschal offering, he said it grazes? One can say this is the meaning: granted, without this answer of Rava he could not challenge from the mishna, since there it is different: if the offspring is sacrificed as a burnt offering, burnt offering status is not uprooted from the mother, as a person can always sacrifice a burnt offering any day. But here, if the offspring itself is sacrificed as a Paschal offering, Paschal status turns out to be uprooted from the mother, from it and from its value, since he can sacrifice only one Paschal offering; therefore the offspring is not sacrificed as a Paschal offering, uprooting [the mother] from what it was designated for. But according to Rava he challenges well: since he holds that because a leftover Paschal offering is sacrificed as a peace offering it is considered as though there were peace offering status for its mother, he should likewise have said, for this reason, that before Passover too the offspring itself is sacrificed as a Paschal offering. And not as Rashi explained, who explained: let him disagree in the first clause too and say that the offspring itself is sacrificed as a peace offering before Passover, since before Passover too, if one slaughtered a Paschal offering for the sake of a peace offering it is valid, for a Paschal offering during the rest of the year, not on the fourteenth of Nisan, is sacrificed as a peace offering; therefore there is peace offering status for its mother.
tosafot:a6.1: Abaye says: nobody disagrees at all; to the place that the leftover goes, the offspring goes: Abaye [comes] to explain all of Rabbi Elazar’s words. With one who designates a female for a burnt offering and it gave birth, and likewise one who designates a female for a Paschal offering and it remained, in these two places he said the offspring itself is sacrificed, since [the mother] is not uprooted from its sanctity: with one who designates a female for a burnt offering, its value will not be pushed away from being a burnt offering; and likewise with one who designates a female for a Paschal offering and it remained and gave birth, if its offspring is sacrificed the mother is not pushed away from being a peace offering, since once Passover has passed it is fit only for a peace offering. But with a guilt offering’s substitute, and likewise one who designated a female for his Paschal offering and it gave birth before Passover, where in both Rabbi Elazar said the offspring grazes, that is because if the offspring of the guilt offering’s substitute were sacrificed, its mother would be pushed away from what it was first designated for, namely a guilt offering, as one cannot sacrifice two guilt offerings; and likewise with one who designates a female for his Paschal offering and it gave birth before Passover, if the offspring itself were sacrificed, its mother, it and its value, would be pushed away from the Paschal offering, as one can bring only one Paschal offering a year. So I heard. However, the wording of the Talmud does not really fit this, and Rashi too did not explain it so.
gershom:a1.1: And he brings a Paschal offering with its money: a male.
gershom:a2.1: If it gave birth before Passover, the offspring grazes until it becomes unfit, etc.
gershom:a3.1: If it remained after Passover: for example, he brought another, male Paschal offering, and this female remained after Passover. It grazes until it becomes unfit, is sold, and he brings a peace offering with its money, since a leftover Paschal offering is sacrificed as a peace offering. But the animal itself that he designated for a Paschal offering is not sacrificed as a peace offering, [because the Paschal offering is his obligation]. And when he designated a female for a Paschal offering, he designated it for its value. If it gave birth after Passover, it grazes, etc.
gershom:a4.1: But here, where there is no peace offering status for its mother: since he did not designate the mother at first for the sake of a peace offering but for the sake of a Paschal offering; moreover, he designated it only for its value.
gershom:a5.1: He said to him: after Passover is different. Why is it sacrificed as a peace offering? Because a leftover Paschal offering itself is sacrificed as a peace offering, [and it is like a case where there is peace offering status for its mother. If so, since you say that a leftover Paschal offering itself is sacrificed as a peace offering,] let him also disagree in the first clause, where it gave birth before Passover, since the offspring is a leftover Paschal offering, and let Rabbi Elazar [Rabbeinu Gershom: “Rabbi Eliezer”] say that it itself is sacrificed as a peace offering.
gershom:a6.1: Indeed so: that he disagrees in the first clause.
gershom:a7.1: Abaye said: nobody disagrees at all: in the first clause, only in the latter clause. And what is the reason? Because it is learned as a tradition that to the place that the leftover goes, the offspring goes.
gershom:a8.1: And when it remained, not set aside to graze until after Passover, since a leftover Paschal offering is sacrificed as a peace offering, as we said: if it remained after Passover, it grazes until it becomes unfit, is sold, and he brings a peace offering with its money, [and the offspring] too is itself sacrificed as a peace offering. But if it gave birth before Passover — for what was its mother consecrated? Only for its value, since [as long as he has not sacrificed his Paschal offering] it is his obligation, and he knows full well that a female cannot be [a Paschal offering, only for its value]. Conclude that when he consecrated it, he consecrated it for the value of a Paschal offering; [and since its mother is] for the value of a Paschal offering, he consecrated the offspring too for the value of a Paschal offering, and its law is like its mother’s, and it is not itself sacrificed as a peace offering. Therefore he does not disagree in the first clause. Another version: but [here is] a female Paschal offering, where there is no peace offering status for its mother, since he did not designate it for the sake of a peace offering but for the sake of a Paschal offering, [and to consecrate] the body of a female [is not fitting], only for its value, as we said; and even so Rabbi Elazar says its offspring is itself consecrated as a peace offering, although there is no peace offering status for its mother.
gershom:a9.1: A Paschal offering is different: since it gave birth after Passover, it is like one who consecrates a Paschal offering during the rest of the year, which is sacrificed as a peace offering; so this one too is itself sacrificed as a peace offering. [And this is] the reason of Rabbi Elazar [regarding a burnt offering]: since there is burnt offering status for its mother, as we find a female burnt offering among birds, it is therefore consecrated in its body, and the offspring too is consecrated and sacrificed.
gershom:a10.1: Let Rabbi Elazar also disagree in the first clause: where it gave birth before Passover, that it itself be sacrificed as a peace offering, since there is peace offering status for its mother [here], as females are found among peace offerings.
gershom:a11.1: Indeed so, that he disagrees. [The printed edition’s editor suggests reading: but he waits to disagree until the latter clause.] But he waited, etc.
gershom:a12.1: Abaye said: this is the reason he does not disagree in the first clause but in the latter clause: he holds that to the place that the leftover goes, the offspring goes. A leftover guilt offering is not sacrificed as a guilt offering after its owner has achieved atonement, as we say in the mishna, but grazes; the offspring of a guilt offering’s substitute grazes too. And likewise a leftover Paschal offering after Passover, [which itself is sacrificed as a peace offering; the offspring too is sacrificed as a peace offering]. But in the first clause, where it gave birth before Passover — for what was its mother consecrated? For its value, etc., as we said in the first version. Rabbi Elazar says: the male offspring itself is sacrificed as a Paschal offering, and we do not establish it like its mother; that is, we do not say: just as its mother is consecrated only for its value, so too its offspring.
gershom:a13.1: Another version: “But a leftover Paschal offering,” etc.
gershom:a14.1: Ravina said: with what are we dealing here? Why does Rabbi Elazar say here that it itself is sacrificed as a Paschal offering? For example, where he set aside a pregnant female for his Paschal offering, so that he consecrated the fetus too.
gershom:a15.1: And Rabbi Elazar holds in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said: if he left it out, it is left out, [and a fetus is not its mother’s thigh], as Rabbi Yoḥanan said: if one set aside a pregnant animal as a sin offering and it gave birth, if he wishes he achieves atonement with it, and if he wishes he achieves atonement with its offspring; and a fetus is not its mother’s thigh but is like one who consecrated the fetus by itself. Therefore, although it [the mother] was consecrated not with inherent sanctity but only for its value, the offspring is nevertheless consecrated and is sacrificed as a Paschal offering. But if he set aside a female and it became pregnant afterward, that offspring is its mother’s thigh and is not sacrificed as a Paschal offering.
rashi:b1.1: That there is burnt offering status for its mother: in the bird burnt offering.
rashi:b1.2: There is no guilt offering status for its mother: since we do not find a female guilt offering, guilt offering status therefore does not take effect on it.
rashi:b2.1: And this too is fit as an offering: and let it be sacrificed as a guilt offering.
rashi:b2.2: He teaches us: that Rabbi Elazar’s [Rashi: “Rabbi Eliezer”] reason is that there is burnt offering status for its mother, and here there is no guilt offering status for its mother.
rashi:b3.1: If so: if his reason is because of the status of its mother, let Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina teach us that its offspring is not sacrificed as a burnt offering, since there is no burnt offering status for its mother, as he called it a guilt offering; and the same would apply, and I would know, that it is not sacrificed as a guilt offering. For if as a burnt offering, where its mother goes for the value of a burnt offering, we say it is not sacrificed as a burnt offering, then as a guilt offering, where neither its mother nor its value goes for a guilt offering, all the more so it is not sacrificed.
rashi:b6.1: Mishna: It may be sold without a blemish: since it is not fit for its purpose, this is a full blemish, and it was not consecrated with inherent sanctity; so it is sold at once and he brings a guilt offering with its money. And although Rabbi Shimon does not disagree about one who designates a female for a burnt offering, where it certainly requires a blemish, that is because there is burnt offering status for it, in birds. But a female guilt offering we do not find; this is the blemish, and it was consecrated only for its value.
rashi:b8.1: Gemara: Inherent sanctity has descended on it as well: for this purpose, that it requires a blemish.
rashi:b8.2: That is to say, etc.: since it requires a blemish even though he consecrated it for its value, evidently it was consecrated with inherent sanctity; the reason it is not sacrificed is only that a guilt offering does not come from a female. That is to say: if he consecrated a male for the value of a burnt offering or a guilt offering, since sanctity of value descends on it, inherent sanctity descends on it; and since it itself is fit for sacrifice, it is sacrificed.
rashi:b9.1: Due to Rav Yehuda citing Rav: who explained the mishna, in that we say “since.”
rashi:b11.1: A guilt offering in its second year: the guilt offering for robbery, for misuse of consecrated property and for a designated maidservant, about which “a ram” is written (Leviticus 5:19).
rashi:b11.2: A guilt offering in its first year: the guilt offering of a nazirite and of a leper, about which “a lamb” is written (Numbers 6; Leviticus 14).
rashi:b12.1: They themselves are not consecrated [kol atzman]: they are not consecrated at all.
rashi:b13.1: An animal whose time has not yet arrived, and Rabbi Shimon said that it is sanctified: as we say in Shechitat Ḥullin, in chapter Oto VeEt Beno (Ḥullin 81a), where it is taught that Rabbi Shimon would say: anything fit to come [to the altar] after a time, one who slaughters it outside [the Temple] transgresses a prohibition.
rashi:b15.1: A firstborn is sanctified: in the womb, which is before its time.
rashi:b16.1: For his burnt offering: it renders a substitute, since there is burnt offering status for it, in birds.
tosafot:b1.1: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina said: And Rabbi Elazar concedes: although with one who designates a female for a burnt offering he said that the offspring itself is sacrificed as a burnt offering, with one who designates a female for a guilt offering he concedes that its offspring is not sacrificed as a guilt offering, even before atonement.
tosafot:b1.2: Obvious; Rabbi Elazar says his ruling there only with regard to one who designates a female for a burnt offering, where there is burnt offering status for its mother, etc.: Here we cannot explain in accordance with Rashi’s second version above and say that the mother’s initial consecration was designated for a burnt offering, since with one who designates a female for a guilt offering too, the mother’s initial consecration was designated for a guilt offering, and by that reasoning we would have to say that its offspring is sacrificed as a guilt offering. Rather, we are forced to explain in accordance with Rashi’s first version and say that there is burnt offering status for its mother in the bird burnt offering. But it is puzzling: how does he make it “obvious” from that? Moreover, above I explained that bird burnt offering status for its mother does not help to make the offspring fit. My teacher sees fit to explain: “there is burnt offering status for its mother” because in the end the mother’s value goes for a burnt offering; therefore the offspring’s law is to be sacrificed as a burnt offering, like its mother. But with a female set aside for a guilt offering, if the offspring were sacrificed as a guilt offering it would not be like its mother, since the mother would be pushed away from the guilt offering and become the value of a burnt offering, and it is not right to distinguish the offspring’s law from its mother’s. And although Rava concluded above, with one who designates a female for his Paschal offering, that Rabbi Elazar disagrees in the first clause too, meaning that if it gave birth before Passover the offspring itself is sacrificed as a Paschal offering even though in the end the mother is to be a peace offering, that is because a leftover Paschal offering is sacrificed as a peace offering, and Rava counts them as one.
tosafot:b3.1: Rather than teach us that its offspring is not sacrificed as a guilt offering, let him teach us that its offspring is not sacrificed as a burnt offering, and all the more so a guilt offering: According to Rashi, the meaning is: if it is not a burnt offering, although there is burnt offering status for its mother in the bird burnt offering, all the more so it is not a guilt offering, where there is no guilt offering status for its mother. And according to the explanation of the RaMaR: if it is not a burnt offering even after atonement, although in the end the mother is to be a burnt offering, all the more so it is not a guilt offering before atonement, since in the end the mother would not be a guilt offering if its offspring were sacrificed as a guilt offering.
tosafot:b6.1: Rabbi Shimon says: it may be sold without a blemish: As for why Rabbi Shimon does not also disagree about one who designates a female for a burnt offering and say it is sold without a blemish: according to the one who holds in the Gemara, according to Rabbi Shimon, that one who designates a female for a burnt offering does render a substitute but one who designates a female for a guilt offering does not, it is well that he does not disagree about a burnt offering as he does about a guilt offering, since a burnt offering has more inherent sanctity than a guilt offering, as a burnt offering renders a substitute and a guilt offering does not. But according to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, who holds according to Rabbi Eliezer [so the printed Tosafot] [that even for his burnt offering it does not render a substitute, and if so,] with one who designates a female for a burnt offering too it should be sold without a blemish, one must say that he disagrees about a guilt offering and the same is true of a burnt offering, and the tanna taught it about a guilt offering to teach us that even so its money goes for gift offerings.
tosafot:b8.1: That is to say: if he consecrated a male for its value, it is sanctified with inherent sanctity: My teacher Rabbi Shmuel found this puzzling: how is it different from one who consecrates [an animal] for the value of libations, of which it says in the first chapter of Shevuot (11a) that it is not sanctified with inherent sanctity? Perhaps one can say that the case there follows Rabbi Shimon, who says shortly below that inherent sanctity does not descend on anything that is not fit in itself.
tosafot:b11.1: A guilt offering in its first year that he brought in its second, in its second year that he brought in its first, is fit, but they do not satisfy the obligation of the owner: It is puzzling, for in chapter HaTekhelet (Menaḥot 48b) it teaches that it is disqualified, its form must be left to decay, and it goes out to the place of burning. Some explain that the case there follows Rabbi Shimon, who says here that they are not consecrated at all, and it speaks there of one who brought it and slaughtered it in the courtyard, which is like slaughtering items consecrated for Temple maintenance inside, which is disqualified; and the requirement that its form decay is so that it not be confused with other disqualified consecrated animals that require their form to decay. Rabbi Efrayim answered that here it is where it was slaughtered not for its own sake, and that is why it is fit, while there it speaks of slaughter for its own sake. We find something similar in the last chapter of Zevaḥim (114b), which says that an animal whose time has not yet arrived with regard to its owner — he is exempt, that is, if he slaughtered it outside; and Rav Ḥilkiya bar Toviya said about it: they taught this only for its own sake, but not for its own sake he is liable for slaughtering outside, since it is fit inside. Evidently, where he slaughtered a guilt offering not for its own sake, it is fit inside. Yet it is somewhat difficult: since here it speaks of slaughter not for its own sake, why say that they do not satisfy the owner’s obligation because he switched a first-year animal for a second-year one? That they do not satisfy it follows already from its being not for its own sake. Or one can also say: here it speaks of after it was set aside to graze, and there it speaks of before it was set aside, and it is a disqualified guilt offering.
tosafot:b13.1: But an animal whose time has not yet arrived, which is unfit, and Rabbi Shimon said it is inherently consecrated: in tractate Ḥullin, chapter Oto VeEt Beno (Ḥullin 81a), it is taught: Rabbi Shimon says: anything fit to come after a time, one who slaughters it outside transgresses a prohibition.
tosafot:b15.1: So too, an animal whose time has not yet arrived is sanctified before its time and is sacrificed after its time: It is puzzling, for in the third chapter of Bekhorot (21a) it says, “And let us derive it from consecrated animals, which are not consecrated,” implying that consecrated animals are not consecrated while their time has not yet arrived. Moreover, it says elsewhere (Zevaḥim 12a): “The night for sanctity, the day for acceptance,” implying that it is consecrated only from the night of the eighth day, but not before. One can say: that applies only from the outset, that it is forbidden to consecrate it while its time has not yet arrived; but if he transgressed and consecrated it, it is consecrated, since we derive it from a firstborn. [See also Tosafot, Bekhorot 21b, s.v. Af.]
gershom:b1.1: Where there is no guilt offering status for its mother: since we do not find a female guilt offering.
gershom:b2.1: [Rather, because] the offspring is fit as an offering: as it is a male. And this one too, the offspring of a guilt offering, is a male and fit as an offering, and I might say: let it be sacrificed as a guilt offering. That is why he needed to say, “And Rabbi Elazar concedes.”
gershom:b3.1: If so: if that is why he said “and concedes,” why did he teach us [that the offspring of a guilt offering is not sacrificed as a guilt offering?
gershom:b4.1: Let him teach us that its offspring is not sacrificed as a burnt offering: although there is burnt offering status for its female mother; and the same applies, all the more so, that its offspring is not sacrificed as a guilt offering, where there is no guilt offering status for its mother. So why did he still say that its offspring is not sacrificed as a guilt offering?] It was necessary, for had he taught us [that its offspring] is not sacrificed as a burnt offering in the case of a guilt offering, I would say: it is only as a burnt offering that it is not sacrificed, since he did not consecrate its mother with the sanctity of a burnt offering but with the sanctity of a guilt offering; but as a guilt offering let it be sacrificed, since he consecrated its mother for a guilt offering. He teaches us that Rabbi Elazar concedes that it is not sacrificed as a guilt offering.
gershom:b5.1: Another version: Obvious; Rabbi Elazar said that the offspring is sacrificed only with one who designates a female for a burnt offering, whether according to the one who says it is because there is burnt offering status for its mother, or because a leftover burnt offering is a burnt offering. But with one who designates a female for a guilt offering, where there is no guilt offering status for its mother and a leftover guilt offering is not sacrificed as a guilt offering, the offspring [too] is not consecrated to be sacrificed, and there was no need to say, “And Rabbi Elazar concedes.”
gershom:b6.1: It was necessary: you might have thought that Rabbi Elazar’s reason is that its offspring is sacrificed as a burnt offering because, since the sanctity of value descends on it, inherent sanctity descends on it too; and with a guilt offering too, let it be sacrificed, since he holds: since he consecrated its mother with the sanctity of the value of a guilt offering, which is his obligation, and a guilt offering is not sacrificed from a female, it was consecrated only for its value; and since it is consecrated with the sanctity of value, it is consecrated with inherent sanctity, and this descends to the offspring, which is fit, being a male, so let it be sacrificed. That is why it was necessary: “And Rabbi Elazar concedes.”
gershom:b7.1: And let us say so too: [since it is consecrated with the sanctity of value, it is consecrated with inherent sanctity, and let it be sacrificed].
gershom:b8.1: If so, if he holds this reasoning, let Rabbi Elazar disagree about one who designates a female for a guilt offering and say that its offspring is sacrificed as a guilt offering, because of “since”; and all the more so about one who designates a female for a burnt offering, that its offspring is sacrificed as a burnt offering, since there is burnt offering status for its mother, or else because “to the place,” etc. Rather, since he disagrees about one who designates a female for a burnt offering and does not disagree about one who designates a female for a guilt offering, conclude that he concedes that its offspring is not sacrificed as a guilt offering.
gershom:b9.1: Mishna: And if his guilt offering was sacrificed: that is, he achieved atonement with another, so this one became a leftover; the money of the female guilt offering is allocated for communal gift offerings, for the horn-shaped collection box, for a burnt offering.
gershom:b10.1: Rabbi Shimon says: since he designated a female, which is not sacrificed, it is like a blemished animal and is sold at once, without grazing.
gershom:b11.1: [That is to say: since a female requires grazing because we say “since,” all the more so with one who designates a male for its value: since it itself is fit for sacrifice, as it is consecrated with the sanctity of value, it is consecrated with inherent sanctity.]
gershom:b12.1: Due to Rav Yehuda citing Rav; and Rava said, “That is to say.” Conclude that Rava retracted.
gershom:b13.1: That is not fit itself: for sacrifice, inherent sanctity does not descend on it, and it is sold without a blemish.
gershom:b14.1: Another version: anything that is not fit for sacrifice immediately is not consecrated with inherent sanctity. And what it says here, “immediately,” is not precise, since this one is fit neither immediately nor later; but because it is about to speak of a guilt offering in its second year that he brought in its first, and of an animal whose time has not yet arrived, which is not fit immediately but is fit later, it says “immediately” here.
gershom:b15.1: [A guilt offering in its first year: such as the guilt offering of a nazirite and the guilt offering of a leper, which is in its first year, as “a lamb” is written about them.
gershom:b16.1: And he brought it in its second year: when it is already called a ram. Or a guilt offering in its second year, such as the guilt offering for robbery and for misuse of consecrated property, about which “a ram” is written.
gershom:b17.1: They themselves: that is, it is not consecrated at all, since he holds that since it is not fit in itself to be sacrificed as a guilt offering, sanctity does not descend on it.]
gershom:b18.1: But an animal whose time has not yet arrived: less than eight days old, and Rabbi Shimon said that it is consecrated with inherent sanctity, in tractate Zevaḥim, in the last chapter, as we learned: one who slaughters an animal and its offspring [on the same day], or a consecrated animal whose time has not yet arrived, outside — Rabbi Shimon says: [it is] under the prohibition of slaughtering outside [the text adds a word, “sheni,” whose sense here is unclear], for Rabbi Shimon would say: anything fit to come after a time is under a prohibition. And since it stands under a prohibition, evidently it is consecrated with inherent sanctity.
gershom:b19.1: [An animal whose time has not yet arrived is different: that is why it is consecrated with inherent sanctity, since it is fit tomorrow.]
gershom:b20.1: If so, a guilt offering in its second year that he brought in its first: why did he say that it itself is not consecrated? It is fit [to be consecrated]. Rather, certainly this is not the reason for an animal whose time has not yet arrived, that it is consecrated because of tomorrow, for if so the guilt offering would be difficult for him.
gershom:b21.1: Rather, this is the reason for an animal whose time has not yet arrived: that he derives it from a firstborn.
gershom:b22.1: Just as a firstborn is consecrated before its time, as its sanctity is from the womb, and is sacrificed in its time, after eight days, so too this animal whose time has not yet arrived enters the pen to be tithed, since he derives the tithe from the firstborn by the verbal analogy of “passing” and “passing” [avara–avara]. But with a guilt offering, where “passing” is not written, it itself is not consecrated at all.
gershom:b23.1: (A printed marker here reads: “up to here belongs to the previous daf.”) Rabbi Shimon says: for his burnt offering, [which is not] his obligation, it renders a substitute, since its offspring is sacrificed as a burnt offering, and there is burnt offering status [for it in birds; it renders] a substitute.
